newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR data suggest government to meet forecast.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR data suggest government to meet forecast.

text.p: Growing tax receipts from British companies and individuals in recent months should help the government meet its 1996/97 PSBR forecast, providing it can keep a check on departmental spending ahead of the general election.

"If the figures for the rest of the fiscal year come in around the same level as last, the government should be on track to hit its forecast," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Cooperative Bank.
The PSBR was 2.6 billion stg in November compared with 3.7 billion stg in the same month last year.
The figures bring the cumulative total for the fiscal year to 13.9 billion stg including privatisation proceeds, compared with 22.4 billion stg in the same months of 1995/96.

"Tax receipts are slowly improving in line with the more positive signals from the wider economy and they should show further improvement, but net departmental spending is growing a little faster than forecast," said Snowball.
Economists said as the election approaches, there is a risk spending could pick up even further as the government fights shy of cutting resources in cherished areas like health and education.

"Stripping out proceeds from the sale of Ministry of Defense married quarters, spending was almost 4.0 percent higher than last year, continuing the slippage seen in October," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Total spending is almost certain to overshoot official forecasts, he said.
The government forecasts the PSBR at 26.4 billion stg and departmental spending of 264.9 billion stg .
Loynes said if spending figures so far this year are projected forward, the overshoot will be around 3.0 billion stg.
And the last few months of the fiscal year are when government departments are traditionally most profligate.
"The last three months of the year tend to be the toughest in terms of controlling public spending, so things could get worse," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
The PSBR figures come a day after the OECD said progress in fiscal consolidation in Britain had been slow.

"Significant further progress in delivering the planned reduction in public sector borrowing will be needed to achieve the government's medium-term balanced budget objective," it said in its twice-yearly economic outlook.
Economists said despite the year on year improvement in the PSBR, there is still a big structural problem.

"There is still an underlying problem with the PSBR. Given the economy is growing at around its trend rate, the deficit is still 25 billion stg. That means whoever wins the election will have to tighten policy," said Snowball.
The general election must be held by May next year.
